title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation
oneLiner: Whether the 1998 prohibition on nuclear power plants should be lifted. Repeal is a separate question from whether anyone would then build one.
body: Two federal Acts prohibit the approval of a nuclear power plant anywhere in Australia. Repealing them would allow proposals to be assessed on their merits under the ordinary environmental, safety and planning regimes. Whether a plant would then be commercially viable, or built in time to matter, is argued below.
contextBackground:
Australia is the only G20 country with a legislated ban on nuclear power. The prohibition was inserted into [federal environment law](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A00485/latest/text) and radiation-safety law in 1998 and 1999 as a condition of the Senate passing the bill that created the national radiation regulator ([Wikipedia overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_in_Australia)).

The question returned in 2024 when the federal opposition proposed government-owned reactors on coal sites. A [House select committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Select_Committee_on_Nuclear_Energy) reported in February 2025 that nuclear was too expensive and too slow; the Coalition dissented. After losing the May 2025 election the Coalition dropped public ownership but, in its [September 2026 energy plan](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-23/coalition-energy-plan-scrap-renewables-climate-laws/107184376), pledged to repeal every legislative prohibition on nuclear and let it compete for the same underwriting as coal, gas and renewables. The new argument for repeal is demand from AI data centres.
contextDisagreement: Almost nobody now argues about safety; the live dispute is timing and purpose. Opponents say nothing nuclear could run before 2040, so it answers none of this decade's price or reliability problems. Supporters say that is an argument to start now, and that data centres give nuclear a customer the grid debate ignores. The Senate would block repeal without Labor or the Greens, and state bans would remain either way.

timeline.text: The ban is written into federal radiation-safety and environment law as a condition of creating the national regulator.
A government-commissioned review finds nuclear could be competitive only with a carbon price. No legislative change follows.
A House committee recommends a partial lift of the moratorium for newer reactor designs. The recommendation is not acted on.

timeline.label: Jun 2024
timeline.text: The federal opposition adopts a policy of government-owned reactors at seven former coal sites.

timeline.label: Feb 2025
timeline.text: A House select committee's interim report finds nuclear too expensive and too slow; Coalition members dissent.

timeline.label: May 2025
timeline.text: The Coalition loses the federal election with the nuclear policy on its platform.

timeline.label: Sep 2026
timeline.text: The Coalition's energy plan pledges to repeal all nuclear prohibitions and to underwrite nuclear through the Capacity Investment Scheme, citing data-centre demand.

otherClaim.title: The ban stops the market from finding cheaper and faster routes to nuclear, such as small modular reactors

claimItself.title: The ban stops the market from finding cheaper and faster routes to nuclear, such as small modular reactors
claimItself.oneLiner: A prohibition rules out every future design, not just today's large plants.
claimItself.body: Cost and timeline estimates for nuclear are estimates for large reactors built once. Small modular designs promise factory production, shorter builds and smaller sites, and several are in licensing overseas. A legislated ban means no Australian proponent can test those promises against local conditions, however the technology develops.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: No commercial small modular reactor has yet operated in a Western country, and the first United States project was cancelled in 2023

otherClaim.title: AI data centres need large amounts of firm power that nuclear could supply

claimItself.title: AI data centres need large amounts of firm power that nuclear could supply
claimItself.oneLiner: The newest argument for repeal: a customer that wants constant, emissions-free electricity and can pay for it.
claimItself.body: Australia has more than 160 operating data centres and over 200 more proposed. The Coalition argues that lifting the ban would let private operators contract for nuclear power for these loads, without any public money, and that a legislated prohibition deters that investment before it is even assessed.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Modelling commissioned by the Australian Conservation Foundation found powering data centres with small modular reactors would cost billions of dollars a year more than solar with storage

claimItself.title: Repealing the ban is a separate decision from building reactors; it removes a prohibition and commits to nothing
claimItself.oneLiner: A repeal does not fund, site or approve a plant. It only stops the law from answering the question in advance.
claimItself.body: Every other generation technology is assessed on its merits through planning, environmental and safety approval. Repeal would put nuclear on the same footing. Any plant would still need a proponent, finance, a site, a licence and public consent.

otherClaim.title: France and Ontario run among the lowest-emissions large electricity grids in the world, with nuclear as the backbone

claimItself.title: France and Ontario run among the lowest-emissions large electricity grids in the world, with nuclear as the backbone
claimItself.oneLiner: Two large grids decarbonised decades ago on a nuclear-heavy mix, with hydro and later renewables around it.
claimItself.body: France generates around two-thirds of its electricity from nuclear and has grid emissions intensity a fraction of Australia's. Ontario closed its last coal plant in 2014, relying on nuclear and hydro. Both are regularly cited as proof that a large grid can run reliably at very low emissions.

otherClaim.title: CSIRO's GenCost report finds firmed renewables the cheapest new-build electricity for Australia and large-scale nuclear the most expensive

claimItself.title: CSIRO's GenCost report finds firmed renewables the cheapest new-build electricity for Australia and large-scale nuclear the most expensive
claimItself.oneLiner: The national science agency's annual cost comparison puts wind and solar with storage and transmission below every other new-build option.
claimItself.body: GenCost, produced each year by CSIRO with the market operator, estimates the cost of building and running each generation technology in Australian conditions. Its recent editions find renewables with firming cheaper per megawatt-hour than new coal, gas or nuclear, and put large-scale nuclear at the top of the range because of its capital cost and build time.

otherClaim.title: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter

claimItself.title: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter
claimItself.oneLiner: The pressure on bills and on the grid is this decade; a first reactor is the decade after next.
claimItself.body: The case for repeal is usually made in terms of today's problems: high bills, coal plants closing, a grid under strain. Each of those plays out in the 2020s and 2030s. Even on generous assumptions nothing nuclear would generate before 2040, by which time the coal fleet has closed and the firming it needed has been built from something else.

otherClaim.title: The political fight over nuclear is distracting from solving price and emissions problems now

claimItself.title: The political fight over nuclear is distracting from solving price and emissions problems now
claimItself.oneLiner: Attention and capital spent on a 2040s technology are not spent on the 2020s transition.
claimItself.body: Policy attention is finite. A multi-year argument about reactors that could not run for fifteen years crowds out decisions on transmission, storage, gas firming and household electrification that determine bills and emissions this decade. On this view the debate is costly even if repeal itself is harmless.

claimItself.title: Repealing the federal ban would leave state prohibitions in place in New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland
claimItself.oneLiner: Three states have their own nuclear bans; federal repeal alone would not permit a plant in any of them.
claimItself.body: New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland each prohibit nuclear power facilities under state law. A federal repeal would remove one barrier but a plant on the east coast would also need the relevant state to repeal its Act, which the Coalition's plan acknowledges it would have to urge states to do.
